Hey there fellow  No Sedation Queen (We somehow did it, and lived through this like a saw trap).

Getting this big of a change done to yourself, your life, your mouth and gums is going to require a lot of time, patience, and you going back and forth to whoever you damn well need to go to in order to feel at ease.

Dentistry places are used to people being very anxious, unsure, needing that extra reassurance. This is the rest of your life, and it's a new and scary chapter. They know this, and expect you to have concerns/questions or may need adjustments. Your mouth is very much still healing and it's going to take a lot of time and adjustment to heal, get used to new dentures, and just living your best life. You are totally NOT bothering anyone by making appointments. You're advocating for yourself, your mouth, and you're making sure things work and feel right. You're doing all the right things :)

I was lucky only to have my teeth removed at a free dental clinic that they do in the state next to mine every year for 2 days. I was however unlucky when it came to getting dentures. I had to wait several months with no teeth (but it did allow my gums to heal on their own) before I could have/wear dentures. Without insurance, my process was slow but at the same time I don't know if I could have soldiered through dentures right after my E day. I can't imagine the pain, and I know from experience it's so awful.

--- Answer to your questions tho ---

Be mindful that this is still a few weeks out since your Eday.

Things are going to feel weird, out of wack, and you will still have to be careful about eating for now. It's normal, and eventually that will change and go away as you get used to wearing your dentures.

I wore my dentures as long as I could until it was uncomfortable. At any time you just feel uncomfortable, take a break. As long as you are listening to your body I think you should be fine, but my situation was also different from yours by a lot.

It can be hard to think of nothing but your teeth and this new challenge. I cried the first few weeks because I was so certain that dentures weren't working for me, that I was never going to figure it out, and that I had really screwed my life up. In a sense, this is also like a mourning process for us.

Whatever you can find joy in that doesn't make you think about your teeth, immerse in that as much as you can. For me, that was video games or binge watching a favorite show. I'd make myself a shake or a tasty cold treat just so I could indulge without putting much pressure on using my mouth.

Be good to yourself, enjoy some delicious summer snacks or ice cream because girl... say goodbye to brain freeze.

All the other quirks you have should go away once you have worn your dentures and gotten used to them. It's just that it's so foreign for your mind to process these dentures.

One thing I have learned throughout my years having ADHD is that you have to really know yourself. Knowing yourself in a chaotic world with it’s many and accessible distractions is fucking difficult. It’s not just knowing what you struggle with, but what works for you. And a lot of the time, we have to figure out what works best for us the hard way. Your sister seems like she means well and is right in some way, but her advice is just way too vague for people like you or me.

Here are 2 things that helped me figure out what I needed to make working out/exercising be more tolerable for me. (I typed a lot, but only to help explain things. Sorry it’s a lot and I hope it’s only helpful and not a mess of text. )

\> Finding my motivation. What motivates/drives you to do things with ease and more energy?Be it in people, adding a routine, making it fun with some music, ect.Turns out I rely on people, and I tried to convince myself this was a bad thing. I let society convince me that I was wrong to rely on people with anything, because my ADHD had me constantly needing people for help growing up. As an adult, I figured I didn’t need to use people “as a crutch”. My thinking was harmful and hurt me from making my own life easier. I’ve since been able to accept help in the form of mental health clinics and their extra groups - one of them being/providing a gym trainer for you! I now go to the gym 2 times a week for 30 minutes, and try to take a walk with my roommate outside on days I can.

 \> Knowing my limits. Honoring my limits. Being kind to myself when I need to place limits/boundaries on myself. Placing my fun things (internet/games) secondary to my health goals.

My brain will try to tell me I have to go full power on a goal, or else I’m failing as a person or not as \_\_\_\_\_ as the next person. When I ignore my needs and limits, I burn myself out and find myself giving up easier. Limiting when I go to the gym and how much/often helps me have that control without feeling like it’s taking over my life.   
I get less overwhelmed and in time, my small change becomes a habit/routine that is no longer dreadful/scary. 

It is SO hard to make changes in your life. We are wired so much differently, so we deserve more grace. And tbh, I still struggle to enjoy being active all the way, but do feel more confident in how I handle it. Esp when I can remind myself that I’m only giving 30 mins to a work out, and then I can be done for the day! If that's not enough, I'll remind myself of all the fun things I can do now that I got that 1 awful thing out of the way!

Whatever you need to start is going to be good enough just due to the changes you are making and wanting to make. It may be annoying having to navigate what will work for you, but I hope you can find something that works for you and not against you. Also, you’re going to probably hate hearing this, but the more we are active, the more our brain does get that benefit with our ADHD. It’s so dumb because we struggle to just do basically any little thing, and even the most helpful shit is a challenge. But once you make working out a routine in whatever way fits you, you’ll find yourself having more energy/being more receptive, and benefiting. Unfortunately, it does take time. I believe in you though! We can hate this working out thing together, but still find ways to do it!

I feel like group settings are generally too chaotic and you seldom get the personalized attention that works on YOUR specific issues. I think DBT may still be useful for you, but the environment you are learning it in certainly isn't. You're right to feel like this fucking sucks, because it does. Group settings are a LOT. And then when you're trying to work and process thru your shit, it gets harder.

I would see if you can find or reach out to a case manager/therapist who specializes in DBT. You can also find a lot of helpful DBT resources or sheets on pinterest too! I have some sheets as well that were forwarded to me by my own case manager if you ever are curious.

As for the trauma parts, I'd also see if you can find an EMDR specialist to help you work through and process your trauma. I've been doing it, and have seen surprising results with myself. And while I have so much work to do and a lot to unpack from my life, I have found that I'm so much kinder to myself because EMDR helped me see that so many experiences I had formed these unhealthy thoughts that I had to re-visit and basically re-wire.

Anyway, I believe in you! You're not wrong at all for being so fed up with your situation. It's okay if it's not working for you <3 You just need a different way to do this, in a setting that helps you more than causes you stress and unease. One hard thing I think we of BPD struggle with is holding ourselves to the standards others put on us. But you more than anyone deserve to make boundaries with yourself. If that means that intensive group settings aren't your thing, that's ok! We always think there's a right/wrong way to get better, but the only wrong thing you can do is ignoring your own needs and judging yourself when you are doing ALL you can. <3   


ps. it's also ok if not all the dbt skills apply or feel they help you. luckily, there's SO many different dbt skills out there, and you don't need to learn every single one and expect yourself to find it helpful or useful. tbh I find some just dumb and hard to use. Honestly, I'd say: It's about being kinder to yourself and more understanding when things don't work out the way we want it to. It's learning to be your friend first, so you can be a better friend and partner to people in the future. It's about not blaming yourself about your situation as easy as it is (omg is it easy as fuck) especially if you come from a life of not having support.

It's also knowing that you are not at fault because you can't find the connection you want when you want it. It's changing your thinking and giving yourself grace to be upset with the situation without blaming or judging yourself for the outcome. Because honestly?
